Is This Why Binding Particles Release Energy?

Consider two particles moving towards each other. If they have mass, then they have some kinetic energy. They have 0 potential energy relative to a point in infinity (nuclear potential energy if they're nucleons and chemical potential energy if they're atoms).

If we assume they're moving with some constant velocity (so that we do no work on this system), then – at some distance – the particles will exert attractive forces with each other. By conservation of energy, this increases their kinetic energies and decreases their potential energy by the same amount.

As they're brought to rest or slowed down (either due to repulsive nuclear or eletcrostatic forces) they bind, and so both their kinetic energues and potential energy are less than in the beginning. This means that they released the energy by conservation.

text:
Can soft-tissue deformation compromise the effectiveness of a roller coaster lap restraint even if the restraint remains mechanically locked?

I’ve been following the Goliath incident discussions, and my friend brought up a point that I’m wondering whether we’re overlooking something important.

What if the issue isn’t necessarily someone’s weight, size, or even a mechanical failure of the restraint, but **how body fat moves under negative G-forces?**

Two people can weigh exactly the same but have very different body compositions. Adipose tissue (body fat) is compressible and deformable. It can shift relative to the skeleton under force.

Think about breast tissue during roller coaster airtime. Even in a snug, supportive bra, breasts can lift and shift out of position. The bra hasn’t failed or come undone. The tissue itself has moved.
**Now apply that same principle to someone with substantial abdominal fat sitting beneath a clamshell lap restraint.**

I’ve also come across firsthand accounts from riders describing their stomachs moving upward or over their lap restraints during airtime. That caught my attention because it’s the exact type of soft-tissue displacement I’m questioning.

Could abdominal fat compress beneath a restraint while seated, then shift upward during negative G-forces, changing how securely the restraint engages the pelvis?
**In other words, could a restraint remain completely locked and mechanically functional while the rider’s soft tissue shifts enough to compromise their positioning?**
There’s scientific research on how abdominal fat affects seat belt engagement with the pelvic bones:
[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9285376/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9285376/)

Obviously, automotive seat belts and roller coaster restraints aren’t identical, and I’m not claiming this caused the Goliath incident.

I’m wondering whether we’re focusing too much on weight limits and mechanical failures without adequately considering **body composition, soft-tissue deformation, and dynamic movement during airtime.**
Has anyone seen research or engineering discussions addressing this?

**Related firsthand rider experiences:**
I verified two particularly relevant accounts:
**1. CoasterBuzz:** A rider who described himself as 242 pounds with a 36.5-inch waist said strong airtime pushed his belly over the top of the lap bar.
[Read the CoasterBuzz discussion](https://coasterbuzz.com/Forums/Topic/rmc-and-weight-loss-motivation)⁠
